newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - March payrolls grab center stage.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - March payrolls grab center stage.

text.p: Bond market investors will be nervously awaiting two key pieces of economic data next week -- employment data and an influential business survey -- for hints about the future of U.S. monetary policy.

The market heads into the weekend after a stomach-churning week that saw the Federal Reserve raise short-term interest rates for the first time in two years and a report of startling strength in February durable goods.
"Being the very first number after the tightening, (durable goods) put the market on shaky ground. It's a little nervous now," said Dana Saporta, economist at Stone and McCarthy Research Associates.

On Thursday, bonds were socked as uncertainties about further credit tightenings and flagging technical factors sank the long bond. It dropped more than a full point as the yield soared well above the key 7.0 percent level to 7.09 percent.
The bond market is now left trying to form a consensus on whether the Fed will raise rates again at its upcoming May 20 policy meeting, at a June meeting, or at both.
The uncertainty means next week could prove to be an even wilder roller coaster ride as bonds react to each new piece of incoming data, analysts said.
"The market will be zeroing in on anything they can grab, but nonfarm payrolls will be the most important," Saporta said.
Economists polled by Reuters are forecasting, on average, 182,000 new nonfarm jobs were created in March, compared to 339,000 in February.

Anthony Chan, chief economist, Banc One Investment Advisors, said the employment numbers will be dissected for any signs of labor cost pressures. The report also includes the unemployment rate, average hourly earnings and the length of the average workweek.

"It's likely to confirm the strength we've been seeing all month. Our four-week moving average has hit the lowest level of claims we have seen in this whole expansion ... If that doesn't spell growth concerns, I don't know what does. It's as clear as sunshine," Chan said, nothing that tightening labor conditions were likely to lead to higher wages.

But before the market can get hold of the payrolls data, plenty of second-tier economic reports will pour in, starting Monday with February personal income and consumption, the New York National Association of Purchasing Management's (NAPM) report, and the Chicago Purchasing Management Index.
On Tuesday, the market will watch for the March NAPM on business trends in the manufacturing sector. Economists expect a slight rise in the index to 53.6 from 53.1.
Also due Tuesday are weekly chain store sales, February leading indicators, February construction spending, and March car and truck sales.
March payrolls are due out on Friday.
With more data, the market should have a clearer consensus on the future of interest rates by the end of the week.

Chan said: "A lot of people are thinking that the Fed's one rate rise may be enough or that there is only one more (tightening) coming. But there is a lot of forward momentum in the economy and one really just is not enough."
Bonds closed down sharply at the end of Thursday's shortened session. The U.S. Treasury market will remain closed on Friday for the Good Friday holiday and reopen on Monday.
Three-month bill rates rose 3 basis points to yield 5.37 percent. Six-month bills added 3/32 to 5.58 percent. Year bills were up six ticks to 6.03 percent.
Two-year notes were off six basis points at 6.45 percent. Five-year notes were off 18/32 to yield 6.78 percent. Ten-year notes lost 28 ticks to yield 6.91 percent.
The long bond fell more than a full point, closing off 1-1/4 to yield 7.09 percent.
Fed funds were seen opening at 6.13 percent on Monday, analysts said, compared to the target of 6.50 percent.
